extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, students of poetics and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and styling epic (epopoeia) and tragic/dramatic poetry: how to use rhetorical figures, word-choices, and how to shape the fable (unity of action) so the poem functions as a single, finished action rather than a history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of foreign (barbarous) words
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign words give loftiness and majesty to discourse when used with moderation and discretion; they make the style barbarous when used too often.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ foreign words sparingly to add elevation; avoid frequent use which becomes barbarism. (Example: Gallic or Tuscan words can lend loftiness if measured.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and conditions of a riddle (enigm)
rubrics_metrics.description: A riddle properly consists in saying things so as to make them appear impossible; this requires (1) a metaphorical expression and (2) that the proposition appears impossible; (3) additionally the subject should be natural and known to everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both metaphor and the appearance of impossibility are necessary; without either, the utterance is not a true riddle. Example given: Samson's riddle fails because it lacks the last two conditions; the glue/tin example meets all conditions (subject known, metaphorical language, appears impossible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionate use of protracted/subtracted/changed words and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Protracted, subtracted, and changed words and other rhetorical figures are allowable ornaments but must be used in due measure and for purpose; the fault lies in their excessive or impertinent use, not in the devices themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a common measure for all ornaments: use them only when they add beauty and are necessary to the subject. Overuse makes diction affected, ridiculous, or insipid. Place figures well and in just proportion to maintain nobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of affectation (excessive use of ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the figures themselves but the continual or too-frequent use (affectation) that makes speech ridiculous; even the finest devices become absurd if employed without measure or occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornaments for occasions where they suit the subject and add beauty; avoid using them merely to display wit. Affectation cloys and disgusts the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate distribution of stylistic devices by genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Different rhetorical devices suit different poetic genres: double words fit dithyrambic poetry, foreign words are proper to heroic poetry, metaphors align well with iambic verse and the stage; epithets belong to the familiar style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match diction and figures to the character of the poem: don't employ devices proper to epic in tragedy or vice versa. Observing these distinctions prevents transgressing the bounds of genre-appropriate style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor as the superior and most generative ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is the highest figure because it conveys likeness and gives new knowledge that other ornaments cannot; a felicitous metaphor shows quick, inventive genius and cannot be borrowed from elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for metaphors that are fresh (neither too common nor too rare) and drawn from apt likenesses; inventing a good metaphor is the hardest and most prized achievement of poetic imagination. Metaphors enlighten and enrich the mind (example: ‘compassion is an altar’ conveys new understanding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty and value of inventing metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: To invent metaphors happily is the greatest effort of ingenuity and marks a naturally gifted imagination; metaphor involves seeing likenesses across very different subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a sprightly imagination; metaphors should be new and apt, deriving from sources that are not commonplace or too obscure. This creative inventiveness is not easily teachable or borrowable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of compounded/double/dialectal words and coined terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Double words, dialectal forms, and newly coined or fanciful words supply loftiness or particular effects but must be conducted by imitation and used with good management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double words especially suit certain poetic uses (e.g., dithyrambic); newly formed or dialectal terms can add loftiness but require careful imitation and tasteful application; do not use them gratuitously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic (epopeia) must be dramatick and active
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitation in epic (narrative hexameter) ought to be formed like a dramatic poem: it must be active, include one action that is entire, perfect, and finished, and consequently have a beginning, middle, and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing an epic, shape the fable so it imitates a single, unified action rather than a scatter of events. The poet should make the narrative 'dramatick' by having characters speak and act to give animation to the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from history: unity and causal linkage of incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: An epic should not follow history's method of assembling many events with only a temporal (fortuitous) connection; instead, incidents of an epic must be so linked that they collectively form one and the same action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting incidents that do not naturally belong to the chosen fable; any episode included should be necessary to explain some part of the action or to serve the poem's end. Do not treat epic as a mere chronology of events (contrast with historical accounts like Salamis vs Sicilian battle examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate selection and accommodation of episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible and skillful to draw many episodes from a larger historical store to enrich and diversify a poem, but the poet must accommodate them to the chosen action so they become plausible parts of the fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use episodes (e.g., Catalogue of Ships) only insofar as they can be adapted to support the single action of the poem; episodes should increase the poem's probability and variety without breaking unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming subjects for tragedy from epic material
rubrics_metrics.description: From an epic's plan one typically finds only one (or at most two) proper subjects for tragedy; large epic subjects must be concentrated and shortened to fit a tragic stage while preserving a complete action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting epic material for tragedy, choose a portion that contains an entire action with causes and effects and shape it to have beginning, middle, and end suitable for the stage (example: selecting the quarrel between Achilles and Agamemnon as a tragic subject).
